Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write a comparison of two approaches to background jobs: a queue with workers, and scheduled batch runs. Around 200 words.

A queue with workers processes jobs as they arrive. A producer pushes tasks onto the queue, and a pool of workers pulls them off, usually within seconds. This suits work that's unpredictable in timing but needs a fast response: sending a confirmation email, resizing an uploaded image, charging a card. Scaling means adding more workers, and a failed job can retry without disturbing the rest of the queue.

Scheduled batch runs work on a fixed clock, hourly, nightly, or whatever interval fits. A single run pulls a full set of records and processes them together, which fits work that's naturally periodic and benefits from bulk operations: generating daily reports, reconciling accounts, syncing a data warehouse. Batch runs make it easy to reason about state, since each run starts from a known checkpoint and either completes or doesn't.

The choice comes down to latency and shape of the workload. If users expect near-immediate results and tasks arrive one at a time, use a queue. If the work is bulk, tolerant of delay, and cheaper to run as one pass over many records, use a scheduled batch. A queue handles user-triggered actions; a nightly batch handles cleanup and aggregation that doesn't belong on the request path, and many systems run both side by side.

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Add a paragraph on what happens when a job fails in each.

When a queued job fails, the worker retries it a fixed number of times, often with backoff, then moves it to a dead letter queue for inspection. The rest of the queue keeps moving. Other jobs process on schedule, and the failure stays isolated to that one task.

When a batch run fails partway through, the effect depends on whether it was built to checkpoint. Without checkpointing, the whole run restarts from the beginning at the next scheduled time, reprocessing records that already succeeded. With checkpointing, it resumes from the last completed record. Either way, the failure is visible only after the run finishes or times out, so batch systems need explicit alerting on run status, not just on individual record errors.

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Add a recommendation for a small team.

For a small team, use a queue for anything a user is waiting on, and cron for everything else. A single worker process handling both a queue and a scheduled task list covers most needs without adding a second system. Add a dedicated batch scheduler only when the number of scheduled jobs or their runtime makes that one process hard to manage.
